screens.title: Gas, Gas Price, and Gas Limit
screens.narratorSegment: Gas is the unit that measures computational effort on Ethereum; every operation in a transaction consumes gas units. The gas price, expressed in Gwei, is the amount you pay per unit of gas. Multiplying gasUsed by gasPrice gives the total fee you pay. This formula matters because gasUsed depends on what your contract does, while gasPrice reflects network demand. A common misconception is that setting a very high gas limit increases cost — actually unused gas is refunded, but an excessively high gas limit can lock more Ether in the transaction temporarily and may hide logic errors. Setting the gas limit too low will cause an out-of-gas failure and revert the state while still consuming gas. For example, a simple increment() call on a small Counter contract might consume a few tens of thousands of gas units, whereas storage-heavy operations cost far more. Practically, always estimate gas for the exact call you will make, then add a small buffer to handle variability. Think of gas price as the priority bid to miners: higher gas price usually means faster inclusion, but you pay more. The key takeaway: separate the concerns — estimate gasUsed accurately, then choose a gasPrice that balances timeliness and cost.

keyIdea.title: Gas basics
keyIdea.text: Total fee = gasUsed × gasPrice. Estimate gasUsed; set gasPrice based on network conditions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Gas Basics
Core Concept
Total fee calculation

The total transaction fee equals gasUsed multiplied by gasPrice. Gas measures work; gasPrice is the unit cost.

Explanation
  • Gas units are consumed by EVM opcodes; storage writes cost the most.
  • Gas price fluctuates with network demand; higher price tends to reduce waiting time.
  • Unused gas is refunded, but low gas limit causes failure and wasted fees.
  • Estimate gas for the exact call and add a buffer rather than hardcoding an arbitrary limit.
Example
// Fee calculation // gasUsed: measured after execution, e.g. 45,000 // gasPrice: current price in wei, e.g. 100 gwei // totalFee = gasUsed * gasPrice
Key Takeaway

Separate gas estimation from gas price. Estimate gas accurately, then choose price to balance speed and cost.

Common misconception
Some developers think increasing the gas limit will make a transaction faster. It does not change miner prioritization; gas price does. A high gas limit only raises the maximum gas the transaction can use.
Why it matters
Accurate fee calculation prevents failed transactions and surprising costs for users. It also informs UI choices when offering fast, standard, and slow options.

screens.title: Estimating Gas with Web3.js
screens.narratorSegment: Estimating gas before sending a transaction is a simple but essential habit. Web3. js exposes contract. methods. myFunction(...). estimateGas({ from }) which simulates the call and returns an approximate gas requirement. That estimate reflects current state and typical execution for the function but can vary slightly when state changes or when other transactions run first. For that reason, apply a small safety buffer — commonly 10 to 20 percent — to the estimate rather than hardcoding an arbitrary limit. A practical example: call estimateGas for Counter. increment and receive an estimate of 45,000 units; sending the transaction with gas set to 54,000 (20% buffer) reduces the risk of out-of-gas failures while still avoiding overly large reservations. Remember to handle estimateGas rejections gracefully: if estimation fails, inform the user and avoid blind retries. Also be mindful that some contracts with complex state can produce underestimates when dependent state changes between estimation and submission. To mitigate this, update estimates right before sending, display estimated cost in Gwei to the user, and choose a sensible buffer. This small discipline reduces failed transactions and improves user trust.

keyIdea.title: Estimate then buffer
keyIdea.text: Call estimateGas and add 10–20% buffer. Re-estimate immediately before sending when possible.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Estimate Gas
Step-by-step
  1. Call estimateGas with the same call payload and the sender address.
  2. Add a 10–20% buffer to the returned estimate to protect against slight variations.
  3. Fetch current gasPrice and present estimated fee to the user before sending.
  4. Re-estimate just before submission if there is delay in UI interaction.
Quick example
const gas = await contract.methods.increment().estimateGas({ from: account }); const gasLimit = Math.floor(gas * 1.2); // 20% buffer
Common pitfall
Blindly hardcoding gas limits can break when contract logic changes. Rely on estimateGas and a small buffer instead of arbitrary constants.
Example scenario
If estimateGas returns 45,000, setting gas to 54,000 provides room for small state-dependent differences without wasting much Ether.

screens.title: Fetching Gas Price: RPC vs External Trackers
screens.narratorSegment: There are two main ways dApps obtain a suggested gas price. The simplest is web3. eth. getGasPrice(), which queries the connected node and returns a current median suggestion. This is lightweight and widely available, but it can lag when network conditions change quickly. External gas trackers or oracle services provide richer data: they often return multiple tiers (fast, standard, slow) and historical insight so you can make predictive choices for user experience. A common pattern is to fetch getGasPrice for a quick default, then optionally query a trusted gas tracker to populate a three-tier choice for the user. A misconception is relying solely on a single source — combining local RPC suggestions with an external tracker gives both availability and better UX. If you use an external service, ensure fallbacks exist when the service is unreachable. Present gas options with clear trade-offs: fast costs more but reduces waiting; slow costs less but may leave transactions pending longer. This combination reduces surprises and empowers users to choose the behavior they prefer. Fetching Gas Price: RPC vs External Trackers means use web3.eth.getgasprice for a quick default and an external tracker for tiered recommendations; combine both with fallbacks.. In practical terms, understand trade-offs between web3.eth.getgasprice and gas tracker services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Gas Price Sources
RPC (web3.eth.getGasPrice)
Pros: always available from your node, fast to query. Cons: single median suggestion, may not reflect tiered priorities or predictive spikes.
External trackers
Pros: provide fast/standard/slow tiers and historical trends so UIs can present choices. Cons: requires integration and fallback logic.
Practical pattern
  1. Fetch web3.eth.getGasPrice() as a quick default.
  2. Optionally query a gas tracker for tiered options.
  3. Offer fast/standard/slow choices and explain trade-offs to users.
UX note
Show estimated fee in Gwei and an approximate wait time. Let advanced users input a custom gas price while providing safe defaults for most users.

screens.title: Nonce: Ordering and Fetching Pending Count
screens.narratorSegment: A nonce is a sequential counter attached to transactions from a single account. It guarantees transactions are processed in order and prevents replay attacks. The next available nonce equals the transaction count for the address, and when you pass 'pending' to web3. eth. getTransactionCount(address, 'pending') you include transactions that are in the node's transaction pool but not yet mined. This is crucial when your dApp sends multiple transactions quickly: always fetch the pending count and then manually set nonces for subsequent transactions rather than relying on the node to assign them asynchronously. A key pitfall is not accounting for pending transactions: if a low-nonce transaction is pending, later transactions with higher nonces will also remain pending, creating a stuck chain. To manage this, track your own nonce progression when sending a burst of transactions, incrementing the nonce for each signed transaction. If you detect a stuck lower-nonce, you can replace it by sending a new transaction with the same nonce and higher gas price. The core idea is explicitness: fetch the pending count and control nonces in your code to avoid unexpected blocking.

keyIdea.title: Nonce control
keyIdea.text: Use getTransactionCount(..., 'pending') and set nonces explicitly when sending multiple transactions quickly to preserve order and prevent blocking.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Nonce Management
Definition
Nonce = transaction sequence number
  • Use web3.eth.getTransactionCount(address, 'pending') to include unmined transactions.
  • When sending multiple txs, sign each with an explicitly incremented nonce to avoid race conditions.
  • If a lower-nonce tx is pending, higher-nonce txs will remain pending until the lower one clears or is replaced.
Practical pattern
Fetch the pending nonce, then explicitly set nonce: currentNonce, currentNonce + 1, and so on for each signed transaction you send in a batch.
Visual
Think of nonces as numbered tickets at a queue. If ticket 5 is stuck, tickets 6 and 7 wait in line until 5 is processed or replaced.

screens.title: Signing Multiple Transactions — Example Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: When you send multiple transactions in quick succession, a robust pattern is to fetch the pending nonce once, then manually increment it for each signed transaction. The provided example demonstrates this clearly: fetch web3. eth. getTransactionCount(account, 'pending') to obtain the next available nonce. Create the first transaction, sign it with that nonce, and send it. For the second, encode the call, then sign with nonce + 1. This explicit control prevents race conditions where the node assigns nonces unpredictably. Make sure you re-fetch or re-check the pending nonce when you attempt a speed-up or if a transaction appears to be stuck. A common misconception is assuming the node will automatically queue outgoing signed transactions in the right order; this is not reliable across providers and can cause unexpected reordering. Also, be cautious with private keys in production — in development you may use a local private key but in production prefer secure signing solutions. By following the encodeABI → signTransaction → sendSignedTransaction sequence while setting nonces explicitly, you retain full control over transaction order and recovery strategies. keyIdea.title: Manual nonce pattern
keyIdea.text: Fetch pending nonce and set explicit nonces for each signed transaction to guarantee ordering and allow controlled replacements.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Signing Multiple TXs
Starter snippet
// Example pattern from the chapter
const currentNonce = await web3.eth.getTransactionCount(account, 'pending');

// First transaction
const tx1 = contract.methods.myFunction1().encodeABI();
const signedTx1 = await web3.eth.accounts.signTransaction({
  from: account,
  to: contractAddress,
  data: tx1,
  gas: estimatedGas1,
  gasPrice: currentGasPrice,
  nonce: currentNonce
}, privateKey);
web3.eth.sendSignedTransaction(signedTx1.rawTransaction);

// Second transaction: increment nonce
const tx2 = contract.methods.myFunction2().encodeABI();
const signedTx2 = await web3.eth.accounts.signTransaction({
  from: account,
  to: contractAddress,
  data: tx2,
  gas: estimatedGas2,
  gasPrice: currentGasPrice,
  nonce: currentNonce + 1
}, privateKey);
web3.eth.sendSignedTransaction(signedTx2.rawTransaction);
Checklist
  • Fetch pending nonce once before a batch.
  • Sign each tx with explicit nonce and gas parameters.
  • Monitor pending status and allow replacements if stuck.
Key Takeaway

Explicit nonces and signed transactions give deterministic ordering and clear recovery paths for pending transactions.

screens.title: Speeding Up and Canceling Pending Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: When a transaction is stuck because its gas price is too low, you can replace it by sending a new transaction using the same nonce and a higher gas price. The principle is simple: miners treat the new transaction as a replacement and will include whichever they prefer. To speed up, resend the identical action but offer a higher gasPrice — common practice is at least 10 to 20 percent above the original, on top of current network rates. To cancel, send a no-op transaction to yourself with the same nonce and a higher gas price — this confirms a cheap transaction that does nothing and replaces the pending action. Important details: set the nonce exactly to the stuck transaction’s nonce and ensure the gas price is sufficiently higher. Also re-fetch the current network gas price to avoid underbidding. A misconception is that canceling always refunds gas; replacing still consumes gas according to the executed branch. In addition, some providers and wallets may offer built-in speed-up or cancel features, but replicating the replacement pattern in your dApp gives you precise control. Always present clear warnings to users about potential costs when asking them to replace or cancel a transaction.

keyIdea.title: Replacement pattern
keyIdea.text: Send a new transaction with the same nonce and higher gas price to replace or cancel a pending transaction.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Replacement
Speed up
Resend the same action with identical data and nonce but a higher gas price. Miners will usually accept the replacement transaction.
Cancel
Send a no-op send to your own address with the same nonce and higher gas price. This replaces the original and performs minimal work.
Practical rules
  • Always use the exact nonce of the stuck transaction.
  • Set gas price at least 10–20% higher than original and above current network price.
  • Re-fetch the network gas price to avoid underbidding replacement transactions.
Common mistake

Attempting to cancel with a lower or equal gas price will not replace the pending transaction and will likely fail.

screens.title: Gas Optimization in Smart Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Gas optimization starts with understanding which operations cost the most. In the EVM, writing to storage (SSTORE) is the most expensive operation. Therefore, minimizing storage writes, packing multiple small variables into a single slot, and using lazy initialization can yield significant savings. Use bytes instead of string when data does not need to be human-readable and use calldata for external function arguments that are only read — calldata avoids copying into memory. Prefer external when function arguments are large, because external functions can be cheaper than public for certain usage patterns. Using uint256 is typically the gas-efficient choice unless you can safely pack smaller types into the same storage slot. Avoid complex loops and heavy on-chain computation when possible; move these computations off-chain and submit only necessary results. Also consider multicall or batching operations to reduce the base transaction costs associated with multiple separate calls. A misconception is that smaller integer types always reduce gas; they only help when packed into storage. screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Developers often make repeatable mistakes in transaction management. One mistake is hardcoding gas limits: when a contract evolves the hardcoded limit may be insufficient and cause out-of-gas failures. The remedy is always to estimate and apply a buffer. Another is ignoring nonce management; sending transactions without explicit nonces risks races and stuck sequences. Fix this by fetching the pending count and controlling nonce increments yourself. A third mistake is not providing users options to speed up or cancel; users can become frustrated if stuck transactions are unrecoverable. Build replacement flows that let users resend with the same nonce and higher gas price. Also avoid excessive on-chain computation — prefer off-chain work and batching to reduce costs. Finally, insufficient user feedback is a frequent UX bug: clearly communicate pending, confirmed, or failed states and provide actions to recover. These patterns and remedies are practical and testable; incorporate them into your dApp architecture and publishing checklist. Key flow
  1. Connect to MetaMask and instantiate web3 and the contract.
  2. Estimate gas for the call and present it to the user.
  3. Fetch current gas price and next pending nonce just before sending.

const gas = await contract.methods.increment().estimateGas({ from: accounts[0] });
const gasPrice = await web3.eth.getGasPrice();
const nonce = await web3.eth.getTransactionCount(accounts[0], 'pending');

// For speed-up
const higherGasPrice = web3.utils.toBN(gasPrice).mul(web3.utils.toBN(120)).div(web3.utils.toBN(100)).toString(); // 20% higher
Safety notes
  • Do not store private keys in production code; use secure signing solutions.
  • Update nonce/pending state after confirmations and clear pending identifiers.
  • Provide clear feedback and an explicit speed-up action for users.

The component links estimation, nonce control, and replacement logic into a reproducible pattern for production dApps.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will develop a practical understanding of how Ethereum transactions are priced, ordered, and managed. We start by demystifying gas: what it measures, how gasUsed multiplied by gasPrice produces the fee, and why neither the gas limit nor the gas price should be chosen blindly. You will learn to estimate gas with Web3. js, add a safe buffer to avoid out-of-gas failures, and fetch live gas price recommendations. We then cover the nonce, the sequential counter that enforces ordering for transactions from a single account. You will see how pending nonces can block later transactions and how to deliberately replace or cancel a stuck transaction by sending another with the same nonce and a higher gas price. Finally, we’ll survey practical gas-optimization techniques both in contract code and dApp architecture — from packing storage to batching calls and doing computation off-chain. Concrete examples and a starter React component are included so you can apply these practices immediately. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you need to keep your dApp responsive, wallet-friendly, and predictable under real network load.

These learning objectives are focused on practical control of transactions and efficient contract design. First, you will master how to estimate gas, set gas price, and define gas limits so transactions succeed without overspending. For example, you'll learn to call Web3. js estimateGas and then add a modest buffer to avoid out-of-gas failures. Second, you will understand nonces: how to read the next available nonce including pending transactions, why sequence matters, and how bad nonce handling causes chains of stuck transactions. Third, you will implement strategies to speed up or cancel pending transactions by sending replacement transactions that reuse a nonce with a higher gas price. This is a direct tool to unstick users when network congestion is high. Fourth, you will apply gas-optimization best practices in smart contracts and dApps — from reducing storage writes to batching calls and performing off-chain computation. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can confirm practical mastery through tests or a small project.

This page defines how to prove you met each objective. For gas estimation, you should demonstrate fetching an estimate with Web3. js and applying a 10 to 20 percent buffer so a simple counter increment never runs out of gas in tests. For nonce management, show a sequence where you send three transactions with explicitly set nonces and confirm they are mined in order; deliberately create a pending lower-nonce transaction and then replace it to demonstrate unblocking. For speeding up and canceling, perform a replacement transaction using the same nonce with a higher gas price, and show a no-op replacement to cancel. For gas optimization, create a small contract change that reduces storage writes or switches an external function to calldata, then compare gasUsed before and after. Each card below lists a short verification step and a mnemonic to help you remember why the practice matters. These competency checks will help you show not just understanding but repeatable, testable skill in building resilient transaction flows.

Gas is the unit that measures computational effort on Ethereum; every operation in a transaction consumes gas units. The gas price, expressed in Gwei, is the amount you pay per unit of gas. Multiplying gasUsed by gasPrice gives the total fee you pay. This formula matters because gasUsed depends on what your contract does, while gasPrice reflects network demand. A common misconception is that setting a very high gas limit increases cost — actually unused gas is refunded, but an excessively high gas limit can lock more Ether in the transaction temporarily and may hide logic errors. Setting the gas limit too low will cause an out-of-gas failure and revert the state while still consuming gas. For example, a simple increment() call on a small Counter contract might consume a few tens of thousands of gas units, whereas storage-heavy operations cost far more. Practically, always estimate gas for the exact call you will make, then add a small buffer to handle variability. Think of gas price as the priority bid to miners: higher gas price usually means faster inclusion, but you pay more. The key takeaway: separate the concerns — estimate gasUsed accurately, then choose a gasPrice that balances timeliness and cost.

Estimating gas before sending a transaction is a simple but essential habit. Web3. js exposes contract. methods. myFunction(...). estimateGas({ from }) which simulates the call and returns an approximate gas requirement. That estimate reflects current state and typical execution for the function but can vary slightly when state changes or when other transactions run first. For that reason, apply a small safety buffer — commonly 10 to 20 percent — to the estimate rather than hardcoding an arbitrary limit. A practical example: call estimateGas for Counter. increment and receive an estimate of 45,000 units; sending the transaction with gas set to 54,000 (20% buffer) reduces the risk of out-of-gas failures while still avoiding overly large reservations. Remember to handle estimateGas rejections gracefully: if estimation fails, inform the user and avoid blind retries. Also be mindful that some contracts with complex state can produce underestimates when dependent state changes between estimation and submission. To mitigate this, update estimates right before sending, display estimated cost in Gwei to the user, and choose a sensible buffer. This small discipline reduces failed transactions and improves user trust.

There are two main ways dApps obtain a suggested gas price. The simplest is web3. eth. getGasPrice(), which queries the connected node and returns a current median suggestion. This is lightweight and widely available, but it can lag when network conditions change quickly. External gas trackers or oracle services provide richer data: they often return multiple tiers (fast, standard, slow) and historical insight so you can make predictive choices for user experience. A common pattern is to fetch getGasPrice for a quick default, then optionally query a trusted gas tracker to populate a three-tier choice for the user. A misconception is relying solely on a single source — combining local RPC suggestions with an external tracker gives both availability and better UX. If you use an external service, ensure fallbacks exist when the service is unreachable. Present gas options with clear trade-offs: fast costs more but reduces waiting; slow costs less but may leave transactions pending longer. This combination reduces surprises and empowers users to choose the behavior they prefer. In practical terms, understand trade-offs between web3.eth.getgasprice and gas tracker services. A nonce is a sequential counter attached to transactions from a single account. It guarantees transactions are processed in order and prevents replay attacks. The next available nonce equals the transaction count for the address, and when you pass 'pending' to web3. eth. getTransactionCount(address, 'pending') you include transactions that are in the node's transaction pool but not yet mined. This is crucial when your dApp sends multiple transactions quickly: always fetch the pending count and then manually set nonces for subsequent transactions rather than relying on the node to assign them asynchronously. A key pitfall is not accounting for pending transactions: if a low-nonce transaction is pending, later transactions with higher nonces will also remain pending, creating a stuck chain. To manage this, track your own nonce progression when sending a burst of transactions, incrementing the nonce for each signed transaction. If you detect a stuck lower-nonce, you can replace it by sending a new transaction with the same nonce and higher gas price. The core idea is explicitness: fetch the pending count and control nonces in your code to avoid unexpected blocking.

When you send multiple transactions in quick succession, a robust pattern is to fetch the pending nonce once, then manually increment it for each signed transaction. The provided example demonstrates this clearly: fetch web3. eth. getTransactionCount(account, 'pending') to obtain the next available nonce. Create the first transaction, sign it with that nonce, and send it. For the second, encode the call, then sign with nonce + 1. This explicit control prevents race conditions where the node assigns nonces unpredictably. Make sure you re-fetch or re-check the pending nonce when you attempt a speed-up or if a transaction appears to be stuck. A common misconception is assuming the node will automatically queue outgoing signed transactions in the right order; this is not reliable across providers and can cause unexpected reordering. Also, be cautious with private keys in production — in development you may use a local private key but in production prefer secure signing solutions. By following the encodeABI → signTransaction → sendSignedTransaction sequence while setting nonces explicitly, you retain full control over transaction order and recovery strategies. When estimating, it calls contract. methods. increment(). estimateGas({ from: account }) and stores the result. Before sending, it fetches web3. eth. getGasPrice() and web3. eth. getTransactionCount(account, 'pending') so both price and the correct next nonce are current. For speed-ups, the component resends the same transaction with the identical nonce but multiplies the gas price — the example uses 120% of the current price for a 20 percent buffer. Important safety notes: do not hardcode private keys in production, and always clear pending states after confirmation.
